stories.actor: Abaye and Rav Mesharshiyya
stories.event: Abaye rode along the Sagya River while Rav Mesharshiyya and other rabbis sat on the far bank and did not stand for him.
stories.turn: Abaye challenged them, asking whether he was not their primary teacher.
stories.outcome: They answered that they had not noticed him.
stories.summary: Abaye was riding a donkey along the bank of the Sagya River, and Rav Mesharshiyya and other rabbis sitting on the opposite bank did not rise for him. He asked them whether he was not their primary teacher, to whom they owed that honor even at a distance. They told him it had not entered their minds; they had not seen him.

stories.actor: Ravina and Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti
stories.event: While Ravina sat before Rabbi Yirmeya, a man passed by without covering his head.
stories.turn: Ravina called the man rude.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yirmeya excused him as probably coming from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are so common people are less careful.
stories.summary: Ravina was sitting before Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti when a man walked past without covering his head. Ravina remarked how rude the man was. Rabbi Yirmeya suggested he was probably from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are common and people do not take such care.

stories.actor: Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Rabbi Elazar moved to Eretz Yisrael, was ordained, and was appointed to the council that intercalates the calendar.
stories.turn: At each step he declared he had been spared one more of the three curses Ezekiel pronounces on false prophets.
stories.outcome: He had been spared all three.
stories.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had been spared one curse; when he was ordained, two; and when he was seated on the council for intercalating the calendar, three. The curses come from Ezekiel 13:9: being excluded from the council of God's people, from the register of Israel, and from the land of Israel.

stories.actor: Rabbi Zeira and a Sadducee
stories.event: On his way to Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Zeira found no ferry and crossed the Jordan holding a rope.
stories.turn: A Sadducee mocked the Jews as a hasty people who still had not changed.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Zeira answered that he hurried because even Moses and Aaron had not merited entering the land, so he could not be sure he would.
stories.summary: Rabbi Zeira could not find a ferry across the Jordan, so he pulled himself across on a rope. A Sadducee taunted him: the Jews had said 'we will do' before 'we will hear' and were still hasty. Rabbi Zeira replied that Moses and Aaron had not merited entering this land, so who was to say he would, and he would not wait.

stories.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of Bar Elyashiv
stories.event: She sued the orphans for her marriage-contract payment and was taking them to court.
stories.turn: The orphans said it embarrassed them that she went in house clothes, so she put on all her clothes, and the clothes she wore became part of the case.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled with Rav that a widow's clothes on her body are appraised and counted against her payment.
stories.summary: A widow in the Bar Elyashiv family was taking the orphans to court over her marriage contract. They told her it shamed them for her to go dressed as she was, so she dressed in and wrapped herself with all her clothing. Before Ravina, he ruled according to Rav that the clothes a widow is wearing are appraised, so everything she had put on was counted toward her settlement.

stories.actor: Shmuel's father, Shmuel, and Shmuel's daughters
stories.event: Shmuel's father posted guards over captive women brought to Neharde'a, and Shmuel questioned the point, since no one had guarded them before.
stories.turn: His father asked whether he would treat them so if they were his own daughters, and later Shmuel's daughters were in fact taken captive and brought to Eretz Yisrael.
stories.outcome: The daughters declared themselves pure before their captors entered and were permitted to marry priests; they turned out to be Shmuel's daughters, and Rabbi Hanina told the priest Rav Shemen bar Abba to marry one of them.
stories.summary: Shmuel's father put guards on captive women in Neharde'a, and when Shmuel asked who had guarded them until then, his father asked whether he would show such contempt if they were his daughters. The words came true: Shmuel's daughters were captured and taken to Eretz Yisrael. They left their captors outside, went into Rabbi Hanina's study hall, each said 'I was captured and I am pure', and were permitted to marry priests before the captors came in. Rabbi Hanina saw they were daughters of great scholars, which proved to be so, and he told Rav Shemen bar Abba to go and marry one of his relatives, brushing off his worry about witnesses abroad.

stories.actor: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai and the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
stories.event: The impoverished woman reminded Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai that he had signed her marriage contract.
stories.turn: He recalled that it listed a dowry of a million gold dinars.
stories.outcome: He wept and said that when Israel does not do God's will it is handed over even to the animals of a lowly nation.
stories.summary: The destitute woman asked Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai whether he remembered signing her marriage contract. He told his students that he had, and that it listed a million gold dinars from her father's house alone. He wept and said that when Israel does God's will no nation rules it, and when it does not, it is handed over to a lowly nation and even to that nation's animals.

stories.actor: Abaye and his tenant farmer
stories.event: Abaye's tenant farmer asked whether he could betroth a nursing woman after fifteen months, and Abaye permitted it.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef told Abaye that Rav and Shmuel require twenty-four months; Abaye ran parasangs after the tenant but could not catch him.
stories.outcome: Abaye concluded that one should not rule even on a simple matter in his teacher's vicinity, because he will not succeed in getting it right.
stories.summary: Abaye's tenant farmer asked whether he could betroth a nursing woman fifteen months after the birth, and Abaye said yes, giving several reasons. When Abaye told Rav Yosef, he learned that Rav and Shmuel require a twenty-four-month wait. Abaye ran three parasangs after the tenant (some say one through sand) but did not catch him. He took the lesson that one should not rule in one's teacher's vicinity, since even knowing the law he had failed to say it correctly.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: They planned to let a woman remarry right away because her child had been given to a wet nurse, as a baraita allows.
stories.turn: An old woman said Rav Nahman had forbidden exactly this in her own case, and Rav Pappi cited Rabbi Meir's decrees against them.
stories.outcome: They admitted they had not had that principle in mind.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua were about to rule by a baraita that a nursing mother whose child is with a wet nurse may remarry at once. An old woman told them Rav Nahman had forbidden this in her own case. Rav Pappi then reminded them of a baraita in which Rabbi Meir requires every woman to wait three months, and of Shmuel's rule that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir's decrees. They answered that it had not been in their minds.

stories.actor: Hillel the Elder
stories.event: Hillel provided a poor man of good family with a horse and a servant to run before him.
stories.turn: One time no servant could be found.
stories.outcome: Hillel himself ran before the man for three mil.
stories.summary: Hillel the Elder got a poor man from a distinguished family a horse to ride and a servant to run in front of him, since that was what the man lacked. Once, when Hillel could not find a servant, he ran in front of the man himself for three mil.

stories.actor: Rabbi Nehemya and a poor man
stories.event: A poor man asked Rabbi Nehemya for support and said he usually ate fatty meat and aged wine.
stories.turn: Rabbi Nehemya invited him to share his lentils, and the man ate them and died.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Nehemya said, 'Woe to this one, whom Nehemya killed,' which the Gemara reads as blaming the man for pampering himself so much.
stories.summary: A man asked Rabbi Nehemya for charity, saying he was used to fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nehemya asked whether he would come down to sharing his lentils; the man did, and he died. Rabbi Nehemya's lament, 'woe to this one whom Nehemya killed', is explained as meaning the man should not have indulged himself to that degree.

stories.actor: Rava and a poor man
stories.event: A poor man asked Rava for support and said he dined on fattened hen and aged wine.
stories.turn: When Rava asked whether he cared about burdening the community, the man said God provides for each person; just then Rava's sister, unseen for thirteen years, arrived with a fattened hen and aged wine.
stories.outcome: Rava took it as an answer from Heaven, conceded, and told the man to sit and eat.
stories.summary: A poor man told Rava he was used to fattened hen and aged wine. Rava asked whether he did not worry about the strain on the community, and the man answered that he ate from God's provision, citing 'You give them their food in its time'. At that moment Rava's sister, whom he had not seen in thirteen years, arrived bringing a fattened hen and aged wine. Rava told the man that he gave in to him, and invited him to eat.

stories.actor: The daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon and the Sages
stories.event: The Sages awarded her four hundred gold coins for perfumes for a single day from her late husband's estate.
stories.turn: She told them they should award the same to their own daughters.
stories.outcome: They answered after her, 'Amen'.
stories.summary: When the Sages set an allowance of four hundred gold coins for one day's perfume for Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, she said to them: this is how you should pledge for your own daughters. They responded, 'Amen'.

stories.actor: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai and the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
stories.event: Riding out of Jerusalem, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai saw a young woman picking barley out of Arabs' animals' dung, and she begged him for food.
stories.turn: She was the daughter of the rich Nakdimon ben Guryon, whose family fortune had been lost, and she reminded him he had signed her marriage contract listing a million gold dinars.
stories.outcome: He wept and said that when Israel does not do God's will it is handed over even to the animals of a lowly nation.
stories.summary: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, riding out of Jerusalem with his students, saw a girl gathering barley from animal dung; she covered herself with her hair and asked him to support her. She told him she was Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter and that her father's money and her father-in-law's had both been lost. She reminded him he had signed her marriage contract, and he recalled that it listed a million gold dinars from her father's house. He wept, saying that when Israel fails to do God's will it is handed over to a lowly nation and even to its beasts.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva and his wife
stories.event: Mar Ukva secretly left four dinars every day in a poor neighbor's door socket, and one day the poor man came out to see who it was.
stories.turn: Mar Ukva and his wife fled into a hot furnace, where his feet were burned but hers were not.
stories.outcome: She explained that her charity was greater because she gave food directly from the house, and he understood why she was spared.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva used to toss four dinars into a poor neighbor's door socket each day. One day the poor man decided to find out who was doing it, and that day Mar Ukva's wife came with him. When the man came out after them, they ran and hid in a furnace that was still hot; Mar Ukva's feet were scorched, and his wife told him to rest them on hers. He was upset, and she told him her charity was worth more because she was at home and gave immediate help in food.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva and a poor neighbor
stories.event: Mar Ukva sent four hundred dinars to a poor neighbor every Yom Kippur eve, and one year his son brought it.
stories.turn: The son came back saying the man did not need it, since he had seen old wine being sprinkled for him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva said the man was that pampered, doubled the sum, and sent it.
stories.summary: Each Yom Kippur eve Mar Ukva sent four hundred dinars to a poor man in his neighborhood. One year he sent it with his son, who returned saying the man did not need charity, because he had seen them pouring old wine on the floor for him. Mar Ukva replied that if he was so used to luxury, he needed more, and he doubled the gift.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records.
stories.turn: They showed seven thousand gold dinars, and he judged this too little provision for the long road ahead.
stories.outcome: He gave away half of his remaining wealth.
stories.summary: As Mar Ukva was dying, he asked for his charity accounts and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars. He said his provisions were light and the road long. He got up and gave away half his money; the Gemara explains that the one-fifth limit on charity does not apply at death.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents and the heirs
stories.event: The heirs of a deceased man claimed a bag of documents deposited with a woman, and she said she had seized it while he was alive.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman asked whether she had witnesses that the man had demanded it from her in his lifetime and she refused, and she had none.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled it a seizure after death, which is invalid.
stories.summary: A woman had a bag of documents deposited with her, and the depositor's heirs came to claim it. She said she had seized it from him while he was alive. Rav Nahman asked whether she had witnesses that he had asked for it during his life and she had refused. She had none, so he ruled it was a seizure after death, which counts for nothing.

stories.actor: Rava and the daughter of Rav Hisda
stories.event: A woman in Rava's court was obligated to take an oath.
stories.turn: Rav Hisda's daughter, Rava's wife, told him she knew the woman to be suspect of swearing falsely.
stories.outcome: Rava transferred the oath to the opposing party.
stories.summary: A woman was required to take an oath in Rava's court. Rav Hisda's daughter told Rava she knew the woman was suspect about oaths. Rava reversed the oath onto the other side.

stories.actor: Rava, Rav Pappa, and Rav Adda bar Mattana
stories.event: Rav Pappa told Rava he knew a document brought before him had already been paid.
stories.turn: Rava said one witness is nothing, and Rav Adda bar Mattana asked why Rav Pappa should count for less than Rav Hisda's daughter.
stories.outcome: Rava answered that he knew her truthfulness with certainty but not Rav Pappa's.
stories.summary: A document came before Rava while Rav Pappa and Rav Adda bar Mattana sat with him, and Rav Pappa said he knew it had been paid. Rava asked whether anyone else knew this; when Rav Pappa said no, Rava declared that a single witness is nothing. Rav Adda objected that Rava had relied on Rav Hisda's daughter alone. Rava replied that he was certain of her honesty but not of Rav Pappa's.

stories.actor: Rav Aha bar Abba and Rav Hisda
stories.event: Visiting his son-in-law Rav Hisda, Rav Aha bar Abba sat his granddaughter on his lap.
stories.turn: Rav Hisda objected that she might already be betrothed, and each accused the other of breaking a ruling.
stories.outcome: Rav Aha said he followed Shmuel's other ruling, that everything is permitted when done for the sake of Heaven.
stories.summary: Rav Aha bar Abba came to Rav Hisda's house and put his daughter's daughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether he did not think she might be betrothed; Rav Aha retorted that if so, Rav Hisda had broken Rav's rule against betrothing a minor daughter. Rav Hisda countered that Rav Aha was breaking Shmuel's rule against making use of a woman. Rav Aha answered that he followed another statement of Shmuel: all is for the sake of Heaven.

stories.actor: Mari bar Isak, a man claiming to be his brother, and Rav Hisda
stories.event: A man arrived from Bei Hoza'a claiming to be Mari bar Isak's brother and demanded a share of their father's estate, and Mari said he did not know him.
stories.turn: The claimant said his witnesses were afraid of Mari, who was a violent man, so Rav Hisda shifted the burden of proof onto Mari.
stories.outcome: Rav Hisda told Mari that this is how he judges him and all violent men like him.
stories.summary: A man came from Bei Hoza'a to Mari bar Isak saying he was his brother and wanted his share of their father's property. Mari said he did not recognize him, and Rav Hisda first agreed that this was a fair answer, since Joseph too went unrecognized. When the claimant said his witnesses feared the violent Mari, Rav Hisda ordered Mari to bring witnesses that the man was not his brother. Mari protested that the claimant bears the burden of proof, and Rav Hisda replied that this is how he judges Mari and violent men like him.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives
stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seized a cow belonging to orphans in an alley, and Rabbi Yohanan approved.
stories.turn: Reish Lakish told them to give it back.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan told them he could do nothing, since his equal disagreed with him.
stories.summary: Relatives of Rabbi Yohanan seized an orphans' cow to cover a debt, and Rabbi Yohanan told them they had done well. Reish Lakish then told them to go and return it. When they came back to Rabbi Yohanan, he said there was nothing he could do, because a scholar of his own standing disagreed with him.

stories.actor: A herdsman of orphans and a creditor
stories.event: A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman, claiming he took it before the debtor died, while the herdsman said it was after.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman asked the herdsman for witnesses to the seizure, and he had none.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the creditor, since he could have claimed he bought the ox.
stories.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman looking after orphans' cattle. The creditor said he seized it in the debtor's lifetime; the herdsman said it was after his death. Rav Nahman asked the herdsman whether he had witnesses to the seizure, and he did not, so Rav Nahman ruled that the creditor's word stands, since he could just as well have claimed he had bought it.

stories.actor: The house of the Nasi and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: Members of the Nasi's household seized an orphans' maidservant, and Rabbi Abbahu approved.
stories.turn: Rabbi Abba rebuked the judges for flattering the Nasi's house.
stories.outcome: He reminded them that Reish Lakish had reversed such a ruling made according to Rabbi Tarfon.
stories.summary: The Nasi's household seized a maidservant belonging to orphans in an alley, to cover a debt. Rabbi Abbahu, sitting with Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, said they had done well. Rabbi Abba, sitting with them, asked whether they were flattering the Nasi's house, reminding them that Reish Lakish had overturned exactly such a ruling.

stories.actor: Yeimar bar Hashu and his agent
stories.event: When a debtor of Yeimar bar Hashu died leaving a boat, Yeimar sent his agent, who seized it.
stories.turn: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua met the agent and told him he was seizing for one creditor to the loss of others.
stories.outcome: The window ends as they cite Rabbi Yohanan's ruling against such a seizure.
stories.summary: A man who owed Yeimar bar Hashu money died and left a boat, and Yeimar told his agent to seize it, which he did. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua met the agent and told him he was seizing for one creditor where it harms other creditors. They began citing Rabbi Yohanan's ruling on that case, and the window cuts off there.

stories.actor: Avimi and his father Rabbi Abbahu
stories.event: Rabbi Abbahu asked his son Avimi for water and fell asleep before it arrived.
stories.turn: Avimi stood bent over him until he woke.
stories.outcome: As a reward, Avimi succeeded in expounding the psalm 'A song of Asaph'.
stories.summary: Avimi, who already had five ordained sons, still ran to open the gate for his father Rabbi Abbahu. One day his father asked him for water and dozed off before he brought it. Avimi stood bent over him until he woke, and as a reward he succeeded in expounding Psalm 79.

stories.actor: Rabbi Tarfon
stories.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could step on him to get in and out of bed, and he boasted of this in the study hall.
stories.turn: The Sages told him he had not reached even half of the honor due to her.
stories.outcome: They asked whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea in front of him without his shaming her.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon would bend down so that his mother could climb onto her bed and step down onto him. He praised himself for this in the study hall. The Sages told him he had not reached half the honor owed: had she ever thrown his purse into the sea before his eyes without his embarrassing her?

stories.actor: Rav Asi and his elderly mother
stories.event: Rav Asi's elderly mother made more and more demands, ending with a husband as handsome as he was, so he left her and went to Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: He heard she was following him and asked Rabbi Yohanan whether he could leave the land to meet her.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he did not know, and when Rav Asi returned, saw he was set on going and wished him a safe return.
stories.summary: Rav Asi's aged mother asked for jewelry, which he made her, then for a husband, whom he said he would find, then for a husband as handsome as he. He left her and went to Eretz Yisrael. Hearing she was coming after him, he asked Rabbi Yohanan whether one may leave the land, and was told no; to greet one's mother, Rabbi Yohanan said he did not know. When Rav Asi came back a little later, Rabbi Yohanan said: you are set on leaving; may God bring you back in peace.

stories.actor: A man in Shihin
stories.event: A man inherited three mustard stalks from his father, and one of them broke.
stories.turn: That single stalk turned out to hold nine kav of mustard.
stories.outcome: Its wood was used to roof an artisans' booth.
stories.summary: Rav Yosei reported a case in Shihin: a man's father left him three mustard stalks, and one split open. Nine kav of mustard were found in it. Its wood was big enough to roof a potters' booth.

stories.actor: A man who rented a donkey, and Rava and Abaye
stories.event: A man rented out his donkey with orders not to take the Pekod River road, where there is water, but the renter took that road and the donkey died.
stories.turn: Before Rava the renter admitted taking the road but said there was no water, and Rava accepted this because he could have lied more effectively.
stories.outcome: Abaye objected that this argument does not apply where witnesses establish the facts.
stories.summary: A man rented his donkey to someone and told him to take the dry Neresh road, not the Pekod River road, where there is water. The renter took the river road and the donkey died. Before Rava he admitted using the river road but said it had no water then, and Rava accepted the claim because he could have simply said he took the other road. Abaye countered that this kind of argument does not hold against facts that witnesses know.

stories.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
stories.event: Reclining in the upper room of the house of Nit'za in Lod, the Elders were asked whether study or action is greater.
stories.turn: Rabbi Tarfon said action and Rabbi Akiva said study.
stories.outcome: All agreed that study is greater, because study leads to action.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were reclining in an upper room in Lod when they were asked whether study or action is greater. Rabbi Tarfon answered action, and Rabbi Akiva answered study. In the end they all said study is greater, because it leads to action.

stories.actor: Rav Yehuda, Rav Nahman, and a man from Neharde'a
stories.event: A man from Neharde'a insulted Rav Yehuda in a Pumbedita butcher shop, and Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and proclaimed him a slave.
stories.turn: The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Nahman's court; Rav Yehuda corrected Rav Nahman's every word, defended his ruling, and with Rav Mattana's arrival confirmed Shmuel's saying that anyone claiming Hasmonean descent is a slave.
stories.outcome: The man was proclaimed a slave, many marriage contracts in Neharde'a were torn up, and Rav Yehuda stopped a crowd from stoning him by threatening to reveal their lineage, so they dropped their stones and dammed the river.
stories.summary: A man from Neharde'a, told to wait at a Pumbedita butcher shop until Rav Yehuda's servant was served, mocked Rav Yehuda; Rav Yehuda excommunicated him, and since the man called others slaves, he proclaimed him a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda before Rav Nahman, and Rav Yehuda went on Rav Huna's advice. At every courtesy Rav Nahman offered, Rav Yehuda corrected his words and his conduct, until Rav Nahman's wife Yalta urged her husband to finish with him. Rav Nahman heard the case. When the man claimed Hasmonean descent, Rav Yehuda quoted Shmuel that anyone saying so is a slave. Rav Mattana, arriving that day after thirteen years away, confirmed it with the story of the last Hasmonean girl who leapt from a roof. The man was declared a slave and many marriages in Neharde'a were undone. As Rav Yehuda left, the townspeople came to stone him, but he threatened to reveal Shmuel's list of the city's flawed families; they dropped their stones, which formed a dam in the Malka River.

stories.actor: Aher (Elisha ben Avuya)
stories.event: Aher witnessed something that shook his faith.
stories.turn: Some say he saw a son die while fulfilling a mitzva; others, that he saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator dragged in the dirt by a pig.
stories.outcome: He went out and sinned.
stories.summary: The Gemara gives two accounts of what made Elisha ben Avuya, called Aher, abandon the Torah. In one, he saw a son die while performing a mitzva that promises long life. In the other, he saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit being dragged by a pig and cried, 'Shall a mouth that produced pearls lick the dust?' After that he went out and sinned.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi
stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, and he covered himself with boils by an incantation, but she healed him by magic.
stories.turn: He fled and hid in a demon-haunted bathhouse where even two people together would be harmed.
stories.outcome: He survived, guarded all night by two of the emperor's armor-bearers, which the Sages explained as a miracle for resisting sin.
stories.summary: A noblewoman propositioned Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. He said a spell that covered him in boils and scabs, but she used magic to heal him. He fled and hid in a bathhouse so dangerous that even two people entering by day were harmed. The next day he told the Sages that two imperial guards had watched over him all night, and they said this miracle came because he had escaped a forbidden sexual temptation.

stories.actor: Rabbi Tzadok
stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok, and he asked for food, so she began roasting non-kosher food in her oven.
stories.turn: He climbed into the hot oven and said that whoever does this act falls into this fire.
stories.outcome: She said that had she known it mattered so much to him, she would not have tormented him.
stories.summary: A noblewoman propositioned Rabbi Tzadok. He said he was too weak and asked for something to eat, and she offered non-kosher food, reasoning that one who does the one thing eats the other. She lit the oven to roast it, and he climbed in and sat inside it, saying that one who does this act falls into this fire. She told him she would not have troubled him had she known.

stories.actor: Rav Kahana
stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rav Kahana while he was selling baskets, and he said he would go and prepare himself.
stories.turn: He went up to the roof and threw himself off, and Elijah came and caught him.
stories.outcome: Elijah complained he had come four hundred parasangs, and when Rav Kahana blamed his poverty, Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.
stories.summary: Rav Kahana was selling baskets when a noblewoman propositioned him. He told her he would go and adorn himself, then climbed onto the roof and threw himself down. Elijah caught him, complaining that he had been made to travel four hundred parasangs. Rav Kahana said poverty had put him in that position, and Elijah gave him a basket full of dinars.
